title: Living because of death
hookLine: because life is short, love now
tomorrow: what can you know for sure about death, and what can't you?

lines: WHY IS DEATH IN A VERSE ABOUT GRUDGES?
cards: A funeral ends, and the cousins' group chat goes quiet for a day. Then someone types: love you guys. Everyone answers within the hour, even the uncle who never texts.
So, what comes first when life is short? An old verse answers, and it isn't a bucket list. It's: stop the fight.
But it hides that answer in an odd spot. Why is a verse about dying sitting in the middle of a pair about grudges?

teach.b: Open the Dhammapada, the old collection of the Buddha's verses, near the start. Verse five, in Max Müller's translation: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule."

teach.h: WE MUST ALL COME TO AN END HERE.
teach.b: Then verse six: "The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once." So why does death show up in a lesson about grudges? Here's the solve.
Every quarrel quietly assumes time. Time to be right later. Time to make up next month.
Time for them to come around first. Knowing that we all come to an end takes that borrowed time away, and the quarrel loses the floor it was standing on. Death isn't the gloomy part of the verse.
It's the reason the fighting stops. That's living because of death: the shortness of life isn't a threat hanging over love; it's the push toward it.
And one detail worth passing on tonight: Max Müller's word love stands for a Pali word that more literally means non-hatred.
The verse doesn't demand a giant feeling. It asks you to set the hatred down.
Love now doesn't have to be a speech. It can be a short message, sent while there's still a today to send it in.

how: In Theravada communities the Dhammapada is read, chanted and taught at temples and at home; some teachers read verses 5 and 6 together in talks on letting go of grudges.

games.q: what does “living because of death” mean?
o: planning every day as if it were the last one
letting life's shortness push you toward love
ignoring death so it can't spoil the good times

games.q: the two verses — tap the pairs.
p: we must all come to an end here

s: in Dhammapada 6, knowing we all come to an end is what makes quarrels stop.
the Dhammapada links knowing we must die with quarrels ending
verse 6: those who know we must all come to an end, their quarrels cease at once.
verse five says hatred ends once the other side says sorry
it says hatred never ceases by hatred; it ceases by love, an old rule.

games.q: your sister wrecked your favorite hoodie. you're giving her the silent treatment and plan to make up eventually. what does verse six say about eventually?
o: eventually isn't promised. set the grudge down now.
make her apologize first; then it's fairly settled.
give it a week of space so you both cool off.
games.why: the verse puts death right beside the quarrel: those who know we all come to an end let their quarrels go at once, not eventually.

practice: Bring one person to mind who hasn't heard it from you lately. In your head, or on your phone without sending yet, find the words you'd actually use: love you, or thank you, or I'm glad you're here.
Then rest with their face in mind, breathing easily, until the words feel like yours.

wordCard.voice: Living because of death: letting the shortness of life push you toward love instead of away from it. In the Dhammapada, knowing we all come to an end is what ends the quarrel.

orig.note: Pali: non-hatred, non-enmity. In verse 5, 'hatred ceases by averena', which Max Müller renders 'by love'.

carryVoice: Pocket this: love now, not someday, not once the moment is perfect. One day left in this block.
